cards.q: What are the lung-protective ventilation targets from the ARDSNet ARMA trial?
cards.a: Tidal volume about 6 mL/kg predicted body weight (4–8 acceptable), plateau pressure ≤30 cmH₂O, and a driving pressure (plateau − PEEP) ideally below about 15 cmH₂O.

cards.q: How is predicted body weight (PBW) calculated?
cards.a: Male: 50 + 0.91 × (height in cm − 152.4) kg. Female: 45.5 + 0.91 × (height in cm − 152.4) kg. Use height, never actual weight, to set tidal volume.

cards.x: Static compliance = tidal volume ÷ ({{c1::plateau pressure}} − {{c2::PEEP}}); dynamic compliance uses {{c3::peak inspiratory pressure}} in place of plateau.

cards.q: A patient on volume control has a rising peak pressure (45 cmH₂O) but an unchanged plateau pressure (20 cmH₂O). What is the most likely problem?
o: Increased airway resistance (secretions, bronchospasm, kinked or biting tube)
Reduced lung compliance from worsening ARDS
cards.e: A large peak–plateau gap means a resistive problem. If both peak and plateau rise together, think compliance: pneumothorax, ARDS, mainstem intubation, abdominal distension.

cards.q: Both peak and plateau pressures have risen suddenly with falling SpO₂ and absent breath sounds on the left. What is the best immediate action?
o: Check for a pneumothorax or mainstem intubation and treat accordingly (decompress if tension)
cards.e: Both pressures rising = reduced compliance. Absent unilateral breath sounds suggests pneumothorax or a tube in the right/left main bronchus.

cards.q: What does the mnemonic DOPES stand for when a ventilated patient suddenly deteriorates?
cards.a: Displacement of the tube, Obstruction (secretions, kink), Pneumothorax, Equipment failure, Stacked breaths (auto-PEEP). Disconnect from the ventilator and bag manually to separate patient from machine problems.

cards.q: What is auto-PEEP and how do you reduce it?
cards.a: Gas trapped at end-expiration because the next breath begins before expiratory flow reaches zero. Increase expiratory time (lower rate or tidal volume, shorter inspiratory time), treat bronchospasm, and consider matching extrinsic PEEP to about 80% of intrinsic PEEP in spontaneously triggering patients.

cards.q: What are the haemodynamic effects of positive pressure ventilation and PEEP?
cards.a: Increased intrathoracic pressure reduces venous return and RV preload, which can lower cardiac output and BP, especially in hypovolaemia. It also reduces LV afterload, which may help failing hearts.

cards.q: Which parameter is the trigger in pressure-support ventilation and how does the breath end?
cards.a: The patient triggers with a flow or pressure drop; the breath is flow-cycled, ending when inspiratory flow falls to about 25% of peak (adjustable).

cards.q: Name the four mechanisms of ventilator-induced lung injury.
cards.a: Barotrauma (high pressure), volutrauma (overdistension), atelectrauma (repeated opening and closing) and biotrauma (inflammatory mediator release).

cards.x: The Rapid Shallow Breathing Index is {{c1::respiratory rate ÷ tidal volume (in litres)}}; a value below about {{c2::105}} predicts weaning success.

cards.q: What are the usual criteria for a spontaneous breathing trial?
cards.a: Improving or resolved cause of respiratory failure, adequate oxygenation (PaO₂/FiO₂ >150–200 with PEEP ≤5–8), haemodynamic stability off or on minimal vasopressors, adequate cough and mentation, low sedation. Trial of 30–120 minutes on low pressure support or T-piece.

cards.q: What are the signs of an SBT failure?
cards.a: Respiratory rate >35/min, SpO₂ <90%, heart rate >140 or a 20% change, systolic BP >180 or <90, agitation, diaphoresis or increased work of breathing.

cards.q: Which patients benefit from prophylactic NIV or high-flow oxygen after extubation?
cards.a: High-risk patients: age >65, cardiac failure, COPD or chronic hypercapnia, obesity, weak cough, prolonged ventilation, more than one failed SBT. Preventive NIV reduces reintubation in hypercapnic and high-risk groups.

cards.q: What is a cuff-leak test used for?
cards.a: To predict post-extubation stridor from laryngeal oedema: little or no leak around a deflated cuff suggests risk, particularly in patients with long intubation, traumatic intubation or large tubes. Consider steroids (e.g. methylprednisolone started 12–24 h before extubation) in high-risk adults.

cards.q: Which cuff pressure range is recommended for an endotracheal tube?
cards.a: 20–30 cmH₂O, checked with a manometer at least once per shift. Higher pressures cause tracheal ischaemia; lower pressures allow aspiration around the cuff.

cards.q: Name the elements of a ventilator-associated pneumonia prevention bundle.
cards.a: Head-of-bed 30–45°, daily sedation interruption and breathing trial assessment, subglottic secretion drainage for expected >48–72 h ventilation, cuff pressure control, oral hygiene, avoiding unnecessary circuit changes or fluid pooling in tubing, and early mobility.

cards.q: What is permissive hypercapnia and what limit is commonly accepted?
cards.a: Allowing PaCO₂ to rise to achieve low tidal volumes and plateau pressures. Usually acceptable if pH stays above about 7.20; contraindicated in raised ICP, severe pulmonary hypertension and significant haemodynamic instability.

cards.q: How do you set an inspiratory-to-expiratory ratio in obstructive lung disease?
cards.a: Use a long expiratory time (I:E 1:3 to 1:5) with low respiratory rate and short inspiratory time to avoid breath stacking and auto-PEEP.

cards.q: What does minute ventilation equal and what does it control?
cards.a: Minute ventilation = respiratory rate × tidal volume; it is the main determinant of PaCO₂. Doubling alveolar ventilation roughly halves PaCO₂.

cards.q: Which of these is a recognised indication for non-invasive ventilation as first-line therapy?
o: COPD exacerbation with acute respiratory acidosis (pH about 7.25–7.35)
Severe ARDS with PaO₂/FiO₂ 60 and shock
cards.e: NIV has the strongest evidence in hypercapnic COPD exacerbations and cardiogenic pulmonary oedema. Avoid it in a patient who cannot protect their airway or who is haemodynamically unstable.

cards.q: What is the difference between PEEP and CPAP?
cards.a: PEEP is positive pressure at end-expiration during ventilated breaths; CPAP is continuous positive pressure through the whole cycle in a spontaneously breathing patient, with no inspiratory assistance.

cards.q: What does APRV do?
cards.a: Airway pressure release ventilation applies a prolonged high pressure (P high) with brief releases (T low) so the patient breathes spontaneously on top, promoting recruitment and a high mean airway pressure.

cards.q: List four causes of high airway pressure alarms.
cards.a: Secretions or mucus plug, bronchospasm, biting or kinked tube, patient coughing or dyssynchrony, pneumothorax, mainstem intubation, reduced compliance such as pulmonary oedema or abdominal distension.
